claims.text: In situ aberration-corrected (scanning) transmission electron microscopy with a heating holder can investigate the atomic-scale thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
High-temperature exposure will induce detectable atomic-scale structural changes in nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Possible thermally induced changes include atomic diffusion, variations in local ordering, and phase segregation.
Nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a homogeneous, disordered solid-solution structure at room temperature.
In situ high-temperature diffraction can identify time- and temperature-dependent phase formation or transformation.
The atomic lattice structure and local chemical ordering can be observed using high-resolution (S)TEM imaging and diffraction.
Thermally activated atomic diffusion or local rearrangement can overcome kinetic barriers in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Thermally activated diffusion or rearrangement can trigger ordering transitions or phase segregation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Ordering or segregation should produce changes in diffraction contrast and lattice-fringe patterns.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will largely retain an equiatomic homogeneous structure up to a critical temperature.
Above a critical temperature, AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will develop observable local compositional fluctuations or segregation.
Room-temperature AC-(S)TEM images will show no significant phase demixing in the nanoparticles.
The onset temperature for detectable structural transitions may depend on nanoparticle size, strain, and local environment.
Selected-area electron diffraction can identify changes in phase composition during heating.
The nanoparticles may evolve through either gradual diffusion or sudden phase segregation.
